title: How We Decide Who Deserves Our Help - Nautilus
gist: A theoretical PNAS study tackles the evolutionary puzzle of cooperation—why costly helping emerged under 'survival of the fittest'—and how groups collectively decide who deserves to be helped as reciprocity scales beyond pairs.

insights.claim: Cooperation is costly and may not be repaid, so its emergence from a seemingly selfish 'survival of the fittest' regime is an evolutionary puzzle.
insights.speaker: Jake Currie
insights.so_what: Frames the core theoretical problem the research addresses about the origins of prosocial behavior.
insights.locator: helping someone comes at a cost

insights.claim: Reciprocal cooperation is simple between two individuals but becomes murkier when scaled up to circles of friends, classrooms, or campuses.
insights.speaker: Jake Currie
insights.so_what: Identifies group-scale reputation and desert judgments as the hard part of sustaining cooperation.
insights.locator: When you scale up that dynamic

insights.claim: How groups collectively decide who deserves to be helped is the subject of a new theoretical study published in PNAS.
insights.speaker: Jake Currie
insights.so_what: Points to formal modeling of moral desert judgments, relevant to understanding social norms and reputation systems.
insights.locator: the subject of a new theoretical study published in the Proceedings of the National Academy of Sciences
